name: Emeka Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Emeka, and thank you for having me. I work as a field researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This is Stonebridge Farm, eighty hectares, and my grandfather cleared the top fields with his own hands. I keep fifty beef cattle, grow maize for silage and make hay, with Grace keeping the hens and the books. Up at six, pray, feed the cattle, then whatever the season wants, today it was fixing the fence the bull went through. I like being my own master and seeing the cattle grow, and what wears me out is the overdraft, which never goes away.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every farm round here runs on one. We borrow in spring for seed and fertiliser and pay it back when the cattle sell in autumn, and in between we have maybe two or three weeks of money. The bank manager is a decent man, I went to school with his father. I don't use computers, I've got a phone that makes calls and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told them so. They were all going on about these machines that think, and it turns out you still need a man to get up at six and feed the cattle. I'd say it at church and at the market, and the young ones would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's what I expected. Farming is about the land and the weather and hard work, and no computer changes that. My worries are the bank and the price of fertiliser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I do. No new gadgets, no apps. I'd keep doing what my father taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use computers. Has that ever cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, with the government forms. Grace does them, or my daughter does them on her phone. I've never yet met a cow that cared whether I filled the form in online or with a pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be thinking about instead, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who takes over the farm. My sons are in the city, one keeps accounts and one fixes cars. That's what keeps me up, not machines.

S0.say: I'd say I told them so, because you still need a man up at six to feed cattle. I'd say it at church and at the market.
S0.think: It's what I expected, because farming is land, weather and hard work. My real worries are the bank and fertiliser prices.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as before with no new gadgets or apps. Keeps farming the way his father taught him.
S0.quote: I've never yet met a cow that cared whether I filled the form in online or with a pen.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka speaks with pride about his grandfather and his independence. He has no interest in technology and leaves forms to his wife and daughter. The real question in his life is succession, since both sons work in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now one with more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but it's not for me. A man should do his own work. If the young people want robots, that's their business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it passes me by. I'm too set in my ways and the farm's too small for anyone to sell me a robot. But I'd worry about prices if the big places get them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what happens to the neighbours first. I'm not borrowing more to buy a machine I don't understand. I'd keep doing the work myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Something in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going your own way. What if the neighbours get robots and you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'll have robots and I'll have my cattle. When the robot breaks down in a snowstorm, they'll be ringing me to come with the tractor. I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would be behind this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies and the city people who run them. They've never pulled a calf. And the government will help them, because it always helps the big ones over the small.

S1.say: I'd say good luck to them, but it's not for me, because a man should do his own work. If young people want robots, that's their business.
S1.think: I think it passes me by, since I'm set in my ways and too small for anyone to sell me a robot. I'd worry about prices if big farms get them.
S1.do: Waits to see what happens to the neighbours first and refuses to borrow for a machine he doesn't understand. Keeps doing the work himself.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, with something in the background.
S1.quote: When the robot breaks down in a snowstorm, they'll be ringing me to come with the tractor.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka's pride in his own work frames everything. He blames big companies, city people and a government he sees as favouring big business. His snowstorm story is a mix of belief and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and people should stand up against it. Men need work, it's how God made us. I'd say it from the front at church if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. If machines can farm better and cheaper than us, the price of beef drops and the bank won't wait. Two years isn't enough time to do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back to the bone the first year, no new machinery, no trips. I'd keep farming, because I don't know anything else. I'd lean on Grace's sister and the church if we came to it, before I'd go to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep, and I don't usually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your sons for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, though it would cost me. A father isn't meant to ask his sons for money, he's meant to leave them a farm. My son the accountant would help, I know he would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should look after each other, like the church always has. The government will come with handouts, but they don't fix a man's pride. We'd need to stand together.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and people should stand up against it, because men need work and that's how God made us. I'd say it at church.
S2.think: I'm frightened, because if machines farm cheaper, beef prices drop and the bank won't wait. Two years isn't enough to do anything.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone in the first year and keeps farming because he knows nothing else. Leans on family and the church before turning to the government.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, which he usually doesn't.
S2.quote: A father isn't meant to ask his sons for money, he's meant to leave them a farm.
S2.fieldNote: Emeka's public line is moral and religious; privately he's frightened about the bank. Asking his sons for money would wound his pride deeply. He'd turn to family and church before any public help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's not right. But with five years, people have time to prepare, so maybe the government won't have to throw money about. I'd tell the young people to learn a real trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried. Five years gets me to sixty-three, and I'd still be paying off the overdraft every year. I think the price of beef drops before the robots even show up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off as much of the overdraft as I could and cut the herd a little. I'd talk to my sons about the farm's future at Christmas. I still wouldn't buy any robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like watching a storm come over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask either of your sons to come home and farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask. My grandfather cleared those fields with his hands, and I can't be the one who lets them go to a robot or a stranger. Maybe the mechanic, he's good with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if neither son wanted it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd farm until I can't and let it go after. I wouldn't sell to a company. I'd sell to a family, even if they paid less.

S3.say: I'd say it's not right, but five years gives people time to prepare, so the government needn't throw money about. I'd tell young people to learn a real trade.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three while I'm still paying the overdraft each year. I think beef prices drop before the robots even arrive here.
S3.do: Pays down as much of the overdraft as he can and cuts the herd a little. Talks to his sons about the farm's future at Christmas and still refuses to buy robots.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but slowly, like a storm coming over the hill.
S3.quote: My grandfather cleared those fields with his hands, and I can't be the one who lets them go to a robot or a stranger.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Emeka time to plan, but the threat feels just as real; his resistance means he'd prepare by shrinking rather than adapting. The farm's history and his grandfather weigh on him. He'd sell to a family rather than a company even at a loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people to stand on their own feet. I'd tell them work hard and learn a trade, like always. And I'd say we don't need the government running everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, so it's less my problem. But I'm still worried for the farm and the boys. It feels too far away to be real, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep farming. I'd talk to my sons about the farm and if one wanted it, I'd start teaching him. I'd wait to see how things go before doing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me so much, but for what comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Where are you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still on the farm, I hope, even if it's only a few cattle. I'd rather be a poor man on my own land than a comfortable man in a flat in town. Grace would agree, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard, keep their faith and look after each other. Machines come and go. Family is what lasts.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for people to stand on their own feet, so work hard and learn a trade. We don't need the government running everything.
S4.think: At sixty-eight it's less my problem, but I still worry for the farm and my sons. It feels too far away to be real.
S4.do: Keeps farming and talks to his sons about who might take over, ready to start teaching one. Waits to see how things go before doing anything else.
S4.feel: Anxious about what comes after him rather than for himself.
S4.quote: I'd rather be a poor man on my own land than a comfortable man in a flat in town.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years, Emeka can't settle, because the threat is to the farm's continuity, not his own income. He offers self-reliance and faith as his answer. He would choose poverty on his own land over comfort elsewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A farm that's been in your family three generations shouldn't be lost because of something invented in an office. What would help is the bank being patient with family farms, and young people being taught trades, not just how to use a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About faith, maybe. People will need something to hold on to if work goes. I think the churches will be full again, and someone should ask about that.

headlineQuote: A farm that's been in your family three generations shouldn't be lost because of something invented in an office.
portrait: Emeka Ibrahim is a 58-year-old third-generation farmer with fifty beef cattle, maize and hay on eighty hectares, living on a seasonal overdraft with his wife Grace. He doesn't use computers and believes in hard work, faith and family. He blames big companies, city people and a government that favours them. He is calm about a plateau, uneasy about steady change, and alarmed by fast AGI because of the bank and beef prices. Even with ten years he stays anxious, because his deepest worry is whether the farm passes to his family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a farm held for three generations could be lost when beef prices fall and the bank stops waiting.
whatWouldHelp: Banks being patient with family farms, and young people being taught real trades rather than only screens.
